content: Technical guidance for implementing toxicity monitoring at sentinel sites is expected to be available in 2013. Routine monitoring of HIV programs should be supplemented with systematic evaluations and program reviews to assess their performance and impact, either comprehensively or in specific priority areas. Social science and implementation research are essential to understand the perceptions, values, barriers, facilitators, and experiences of service recipients and communities in delivering and receiving services. Measuring impact indicators such as incidence, morbidity, and mortality can be challenging. Recently developed guidance on using assays for recent infection to estimate HIV incidence at the population level is available, and guidance on monitoring mortality, including causes of death, will be released in 2013. Mathematical modeling is often used to project scenarios for program planning and impact evaluation. Robust data are crucial for estimating the prevention impact of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs at the population level, as multiple information sources and uncertainties are involved. Specific data collection efforts and models tailored to particular contexts may yield more accurate estimates. HIV drug resistance poses a significant threat to the success of national HIV programs. Resistance leads to faster virological failure in individuals on first-line regimens and increases the need for second-line regimens, which may have higher toxicity, more adverse events, poorer adherence, and greater costs. Surveillance of drug resistance should be an integral part of national HIV programs, informing the selection of firstand second-line ART regimens and ARV drugs for PMTCT to optimize treatment outcomes within a public health approach. The World Health Organization (WHO) and its partners have developed a standardized and complementary assessment strategy for countries to implement, covering both adult and pediatric populations. This strategy includes monitoring early warning indicators for HIV drug resistance, which use existing clinic and pharmacy records to assess factors associated with resistance emergence, such as ART prescribing practices, drug supply continuity, adherence to ARV regimens, retention in care, and viral load suppression when available. These indicators should be integrated into national monitoring and evaluation systems to address practices that may lead to poor outcomes and resistance. Surveys to monitor acquired HIV drug resistance and associated factors in populations receiving ART are conducted using a standardized WHO protocol. These surveys assess population-level virological suppression and the emergence of resistance among treated populations. Regularly performed at representative sites, they provide evidence for programmatic and clinical actions to minimize resistance and optimize the selection of firstand second-line ARV regimens. Similarly, surveillance of pre-treatment HIV drug resistance provides nationally representative estimates of resistance in populations initiating therapy. These surveys, conducted at representative ART clinics, support decision-making at national, regional, and global levels regarding first-line regimen choices. Surveillance of transmitted HIV drug resistance among recently infected individuals provides estimates of resistance in these populations, contributing to ART policy decisions, including ARV regimen guidelines and HIV prophylaxis strategies. Surveillance of HIV drug resistance among children under 18 months of age, using a WHO protocol, estimates the national prevalence of resistance among infants diagnosed with HIV through early infant diagnosis testing. National strategies for assessing HIV drug resistance should be developed and routinely implemented as part of comprehensive HIV treatment programs. Recommendations in these guidelines may require adaptations to monitoring and evaluation systems. Guidance is available on the 12 components of a monitoring and evaluation system, along with tools to review and strengthen national HIV monitoring and evaluation systems. Specific areas for review include alignment with new ARV guidelines.
